doc.title: DeFranco Buddy — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: The only white man in Basie's band and the Soundies film
summary: He took static for being the only white member, and a film short had Marshall Royal mime his clarinet solo.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: And you were the only white guy in the band, I know you certainly some…

I was the only white guy and it got to be ridiculous because we never thought about it until we get some phone calls that were nasty or somebody in the audience might, “How come you’re playing with?” You know, it’s really dumb, really dumb because we were almost like a family and I got a lot of static for being the only white guy in the band. And also they were doing these Soundie, sound, I forget what, short subjects on television, Soundies I think there were called.

Yeah, right, for the shorts. And they had decided, the company decided, that they didn’t want me filmed on it because they’re going to try to sell them, Soundies—the shorts—down south, so they needed a black guy. So I played the background, I played the soundtrack, then they had Marshall Royal come in and simulate what I was playing. The whole thing was stupid because Marshall Royal looked more white than I did. So the whole thing didn’t make any sense.
How did Basie feel about it, did he take any position either way?

Well, he was pragmatic and he was kind of a guy that a lot of things he lived with, he lived with, and that was it. For questions, he wasn’t going to stop the whole session because of this. “It’s ok, well, you know, we’ll hire Marshall.” And he said to me, “Ok by you?” “Yeah, sure.” But the strangest thing about that too, was many later years, I was told that a lot of people liked Marshall’s playing on that session [laughter], and Marshall wouldn’t say it wasn’t me, he would just say “Oh, thanks.”
Oh, he never gave it up?
Who knows? Maybe he thought he played it.
